newsitem.title: UK: Her indoors joins squeegee bandit in UK dictionary.
newsitem.headline: Her indoors joins squeegee bandit in UK dictionary.

text.p: Her indoors gave the squeegee bandit a good laldy, fearing he was a badass.
According to Britain's most famous dictionary this is perfectly acceptable modern English.

From minty and stonker to leopon and meme, the Oxford English Dictionary is determined to keep up with the times and on Thursday publishes the latest addition to what it claims is the "supreme treasure-house of the English language".

The 3,000 new words and meanings have been collected by a network of 60 readers around the world. They were only included after research by Oxford lexicographers and consultations with a 150-strong team of international specialists.

Job clubs, Clintonomics and the internal market are included for the first time as are nanotechnology and limacologist -- a slug expert. A leopon is a leopard/lion cross while a meme is an element of a culture that can be passed on by non-genetic means.

Many new terms come from the fringes of society like squeegee bandit -- someone who washes a car window at a traffic light and demands payment -- and swallowers, a smuggler who swallows drugs to get them through customs.
Vanilla has entered the dictionary as meaning unadventurous and minty is another word for gay. British television has made "her indoors" -- one's wife or girlfriend -- part of the language.
Luvvy is officially recognised by the dictionary as referring to an actor or actress and stonker means "something which is very large or impressive of its kind".
But the dictionary says many of the new terms are not really new at all. Laldy, meaning a beating, can be traced back to 1889.
And a badass? It's a latter-day troublemaker.
